name: TypeScript Basics
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: Why types help, inference, interfaces, typed functions, unions and narrowing, strict null checks, generics and reading compiler errors.

lesson.intro: TypeScript is JavaScript with a type system on top: its compiler catches typos, wrong arguments and possibly undefined values before anything runs. This lesson covers inference, object and function types, unions and narrowing, null checks, generics, utility types and compiler errors.
objectives: Explain what the compiler checks and what disappears at runtime
Annotate parameters, objects and functions, and let inference handle the rest
Narrow unions with typeof, in and discriminant checks, and handle null safely
Write generic functions with constraints and use utility types such as Partial and Pick
Read common compiler errors and fix their cause instead of silencing them

sections.title: Why TypeScript?
sections.key: TypeScript's compiler checks types before the code runs and then erases them, so it catches typos and wrong arguments but never validates data at runtime.
sections.body:
You rename `fullname` to `fullName`, and three files away a function still reads `user.fullname`. JavaScript prints `Hello, undefined` in production. **TypeScript**, JavaScript plus a type system, flags it while you type.

[[visual]]

The compiler catches the boring bugs that reach production: a property typo, arguments in the wrong order, a value that might be undefined, a caller a refactor missed. You also get accurate autocomplete, safe renames and signatures that document themselves.

TypeScript is **structural**: a value matches a type if it has the right shape, whatever it is called.

Configure the compiler in `tsconfig.json` and turn on `"strict": true` from day one: it enables strict null checks and `noImplicitAny`. Most frameworks (React with Vite, Next.js, Angular, NestJS) start projects in TypeScript.

visual.title: From TypeScript to running code
visual.caption: Nothing about types exists at runtime, so a value from an API in the wrong shape is not stopped by TypeScript alone.

sections.pitfall: Assuming TypeScript validates data at runtime. Types are erased, so JSON from an API can still have any shape; check it where it enters your program.

activity.title: The bug TypeScript would catch
activity.prompt: This is plain JavaScript, so nothing stops the typo: run it and see undefined. Fix the property name. With an interface for user, the TypeScript compiler would have flagged this line before the code ever ran.

props.task: Make the program log exactly: Hello, Ada Lovelace

check.question: A value from an API has the wrong shape, but your TypeScript code compiled without errors. What happens at runtime?
choices: TypeScript throws a TypeError as soon as the value arrives
The value is converted to the declared type
Nothing special: types were erased, so the JavaScript runs with whatever value it got
The program refuses to start
check.explanation: The compiler only checks the code you wrote; the output is plain JavaScript with no type information. Data from outside must be validated at runtime with real checks.

sections.title: Annotations and inference
sections.key: TypeScript infers types from starting values, so annotate only what it cannot infer, such as parameters; note that `const` infers literal types.
sections.body:
You do not write types everywhere. TypeScript **infers** them: `let count = 0` is already a `number`, and assigning a string later is an error.

An **annotation** is a colon and a type: `let label: string`. Write one where there is nothing to infer from: function parameters (strict mode reports an unannotated one as implicitly `any`), variables with no starting value, and places where you want a check against an intended type.

[[visual]]

The basic types are `string`, `number` (no separate int or float), `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `bigint` and `symbol`. Arrays are `number[]` or `Array<number>`, and a **tuple** such as `[string, number]` fixes the length and each position's type.

Annotate the edges (parameters, exported functions, outside data) and let inference handle the inside.

visual.title: What inference picks
rows: `string`: a let could later hold any string
`"dark"`, a **literal type**: a const never changes
`config.mode` is `string`: a property can be reassigned
Returns `number`: return types are inferred too

sections.pitfall: Annotating with a type wider than the truth, such as `let status: string` when only three values are valid. You throw away checking; use a literal union instead.

check.question: What type does TypeScript infer for let price = 9.99?
choices: any
number
float
check.explanation: let can be reassigned, so the literal widens to number. TypeScript has no separate float type, and only const price = 9.99 would get the literal type 9.99.

sections.title: Typing objects: interfaces and type aliases
sections.key: Name object shapes with an interface or a type alias; `?` marks optional properties, `readonly` blocks reassignment, and extra properties are flagged only in object literals.
sections.body:
Most data is objects, so describing object shapes is most of everyday TypeScript. There are two ways to name a shape:

[[visual]]

Pick one convention and keep it; many teams use interfaces for object shapes and type aliases for everything else.

[[visual 2]]

Because typing is structural, you can pass an object with extra properties when it is stored in a variable first. An object literal written directly where a type is expected gets an **excess property check**, because extra properties there are usually typos.

For dictionaries with keys you do not know ahead of time, use `Record<string, number>` or an index signature such as `{ [name: string]: number }`.

items.title: Type alias
points: Can name any type: unions (`type ID = string | number`), tuples, primitives

visual.title: Property modifiers
rows: **Optional**: its type is `string | undefined`, so handle the missing case before using it
Cannot be assigned after creation (a compile-time rule only)

sections.pitfall: Making properties optional just to silence errors when creating objects. Every `?` forces every reader to handle the missing case; keep optional only what truly is.

check.question: In the code above, what is the type of u.email?
choices: string
string | undefined
undefined
any
check.explanation: An optional property may be missing, so its type includes undefined. You must check it, or use u.email?.length, before calling string methods on it.

sections.title: Typing functions
sections.key: Annotate parameters and optionally the return type, so every call is checked; a function type such as `(a: number) => string` describes callbacks.
sections.body:
A function's signature is a contract: what it accepts and what it returns. TypeScript writes it down and checks it at every call site.

Annotate each parameter, and optionally the return type: `function formatPrice(amount: number, currency: string): string`. If one code path forgets to return, the compiler reports it at the function, not at a distant caller.

[[visual]]

Functions are values, so they have types: `(a: number, b: number) => number`. Use them for callbacks and named signatures (`type Comparator = ...`). An arrow passed where a function type is expected gets its parameter types from context, so `items.map(item => item.id)` needs no annotations.

Change a parameter from `string` to `number` and every caller that needs updating shows an error.

visual.title: Signature pieces
rows: Optional: may be left out, and its type includes `undefined`
A default; the type is inferred from it
Optional and defaulted parameters come after the required ones
The function never returns, because it always throws

sections.pitfall: Leaving a parameter unannotated. Under strict mode it is an error (implicitly any); without strict mode it silently becomes any and nothing about it is checked.

check.question: What does the function type (item: string) => void describe?
choices: A function that takes a string and whose return value isn't used
A function that returns a string
A function that must throw an error
A variable that holds either a string or nothing
check.explanation: Parameters go inside the parentheses and the return type after the arrow. void means callers shouldn't rely on any returned value; never would mean the function never returns.

sections.title: Unions, literal types and narrowing
sections.key: A union means one of several types; narrow it with a check the compiler understands, such as `typeof`, `in` or a shared `kind` field, before using member-specific features.
sections.body:
A request is `"idle"`, `"loading"` or `"done"`; a shape is a circle or a square. **Union types** describe exactly these.

A union of **literal types**, `type Status = "idle" | "loading" | "done"`, allows only those values, so `"Done"` is a compile error: the cure for magic strings.

On a union you can only use what every member supports. To go further, **narrow** it:

[[visual]]

Inside the `if` the type is narrowed, and after an early `return` the rest of the function sees what is left. These checks are ordinary JavaScript, so types and runtime behavior stay in sync.

The best pattern is the **discriminated union**: every member has a literal field like `kind`. Switch on it, and in `default` assign the value to a `never` variable, so an unhandled new member becomes a compile error there.

visual.title: Narrowing checks
rows: Class instances (not interfaces or type aliases: they do not exist at runtime)
Objects that differ by a property
A discriminated union, by its literal field

sections.pitfall: Using `instanceof` with an interface or type alias. Those do not exist at runtime, so the compiler reports that the name only refers to a type; use `in` or a discriminant field.

activity.title: Narrowing is real JavaScript
activity.prompt: TypeScript's narrowing relies on checks that also run at runtime. Use typeof for the string and number cases and Array.isArray for the list, returning a different description for each.

props.task: Make the program log text: HI, then number: 3.14 (two decimals), then list of 2.

check.question: Given type Status = "idle" | "done", what happens with let s: Status = "Done"?
choices: It compiles, because string comparison ignores case
It compiles and s becomes "done"
It compiles, but throws at runtime
Compile error: "Done" is not assignable to Status
check.explanation: A literal type matches one exact string, case included. "Done" is not one of the allowed values, so the compiler rejects it (and even suggests "done"). Nothing is checked or converted at runtime.

sections.title: Strict null checks
sections.key: Under strict null checks a possibly missing value says so in its type, and you must narrow it with a check, `?.` or `??` before use; `!` only silences the compiler.
sections.body:
"Cannot read properties of undefined" is one of the most common production errors. With `strictNullChecks` (part of `strict`), `string` means a real string, and a value that might be missing says so: `string | undefined`, `User | null`.

Many built-ins return these: `array.find()` gives `T | undefined` because nothing may match, and `document.getElementById()` gives `HTMLElement | null`.

[[visual]]

The **non-null assertion** `el!.textContent` tells the compiler "trust me". It adds no runtime check, so if you are wrong the program crashes exactly as plain JavaScript would.

Design for it: return `undefined` for "not found" instead of -1, keep optional fields to those that truly are, and validate data where it enters.

visual.title: Handling a possibly missing value
rows: Narrows to `User` inside the block, or for the rest of the function
Optional chaining: stops and gives `undefined` if anything is missing
A fallback: the result type is plain `string`
Calls or indexes only if the value exists
Silences the compiler with no runtime check: avoid it

sections.pitfall: Sprinkling `!` to make null errors go away. The compiler stops complaining, but the crash it was warning you about is still there.

activity.title: Handle the missing cases
activity.prompt: Run it: the second call crashes because Linus has no address, and the third because find returns undefined. Use optional chaining and ?? so every missing step falls back to unknown.

props.task: Make the program log London, then unknown, then unknown.

check.question: users.find(u => u.id === id) has type User | undefined. Why does TypeScript include undefined?
choices: Because users might be declared with let
Because find returns undefined when no item matches, so callers must handle that case
Because arrays can contain holes
Because the callback might throw
check.explanation: The type reflects real behavior: when nothing matches, find returns undefined. Strict null checks make you narrow before reading properties, which turns a runtime crash into a compile error.

sections.title: Generics
sections.key: A type parameter like `<T>` lets one function or type work with many types while keeping the link between input and output types, which `any` throws away.
sections.body:
A function returns the first item of an array. Typed with `any`, callers get `any` back and lose all checking; typed with `number[]`, it only works for numbers. **Generics** fix both.

A **type parameter** is a placeholder declared in angle brackets: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined`. Call `first([10, 20])` and TypeScript infers `T = number`, so the result is `number | undefined`.

[[visual]]

When there is nothing to infer from, pass the type yourself: `new Map<string, number>()`, or `useState<User | null>(null)` in React.

Inside a generic function nothing is known about T. To use a property, add a **constraint**: `<T extends { length: number }>` accepts strings and arrays and rejects numbers.

If a function only ever handles one type, a plain annotation is clearer.

visual.title: Generics you will meet
rows: `interface ApiResponse<T> { data: T; error: string | null }`
One definition for every endpoint's response

sections.pitfall: Reaching for `any` to make a reusable function compile. It accepts everything but returns `any`, so every caller loses checking; a type parameter keeps it.

check.question: What is T inferred as in first([true, false])?
choices: boolean
any
true
unknown
check.explanation: The argument is a boolean[], so T is boolean and the result type is boolean | undefined. Inference fills in T; you did not need to write first<boolean>.

sections.title: any, unknown, utility types and common errors
sections.key: Prefer `unknown` to `any` for outside data, build related types with utilities like `Partial` and `Pick`, and fix the cause of a compiler error instead of silencing it.
sections.body:
Sometimes you truly do not know a value's type: `JSON.parse` output, an API response, a message from another window.

[[visual]]

**Utility types** build new types from existing ones, so a change to the original flows through automatically:

[[visual 2]]

Compiler messages are long, but the first line usually says it all:

[[visual 3]]

Fix the cause, not the symptom: `as any` or `!` removes the red line and leaves the bug.

items.title: any
points: Switches checking off: any property, call or assignment goes
Spreads: whatever you derive from it is `any` too

items.title: unknown
points: Accepts any value but allows almost nothing
Narrow it first with `typeof`, `in`, `instanceof` or a check function
The safe choice for data from outside

visual.title: Utility types
rows: Every property optional: suits update payloads
Every property except the listed ones

visual.title: Common compiler errors
rows: A value of the wrong type, often a missing or misspelled property deeper inside
`Argument of type 'X' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Y'` (TS2345)
The same mismatch at a function call
A typo, or a property only some union members have

sections.pitfall: Fixing an error with `as any`. The message goes away, the checking for that value goes away with it, and the bug stays.

activity.title: Validate unknown data
activity.prompt: In TypeScript, JSON.parse output is best treated as unknown and checked before use. Write isUser with typeof checks: a non-null object whose name is a string and whose age is a number. In TypeScript its signature would be isUser(value: unknown): value is User.

props.task: Make the program log ok Ada, then rejected, then rejected.

check.question: With User as above, what does Omit<User, "email"> describe?
choices: { email: string }
{ id?: number; name?: string; email?: string }
{ id: number; name: string }
{ id: number; name: string; email?: string }
check.explanation: Omit removes the listed keys and keeps the rest unchanged. The all-optional version is what Partial<User> gives, and { email: string } is what Pick<User, "email"> gives.

keyTerms.definition: A colon and a type after a name, such as count: number, stating what it may hold.
TypeScript working out a type from a value, so let n = 0 is a number without an annotation.
The compiler removing all types, so the output is plain JavaScript with no runtime type checks.
A value matches a type if it has the required shape, regardless of its name or origin.
A named description of an object's shape that can extend other interfaces.
A type that allows one exact value, such as "left" or 42.
A value that may be one of several types, written A | B.
Refining a union to one member with checks such as typeof, in or a discriminant field.
A compiler mode where null and undefined must appear in a type before a value may hold them.
A type parameter such as T that lets code work with many types while keeping them precise.
A type that accepts any value but must be narrowed before use; the safe alternative to any.
A built-in type that transforms another, such as Partial, Pick, Omit or Record.

summary: TypeScript checks code before it runs, then erases the types, so outside data still needs runtime checks.
Annotate parameters and edges, let inference handle locals, and turn on strict mode.
Describe objects with interfaces or type aliases, with ? for optional and readonly for fixed properties.
Narrow unions with typeof, in and discriminant checks; make switches exhaustive with never.
Handle missing values with checks, ?. and ?? instead of the ! assertion.
Generics keep types precise across reusable code; prefer unknown to any.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a JavaScript developer what TypeScript would have caught in a bug where user.fullname printed undefined, why the types disappear when the code runs, and why unknown is safer than any for data from an API.

questions.question: What does the compiler report for this code?
questions.code:
let count = 0;
count = "zero";
choices: Nothing; count becomes a string
Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
Parameter 'count' implicitly has an 'any' type.
Nothing at compile time, but a TypeError at runtime
questions.explanation: count is inferred as number from its initial value 0, so assigning a string is a compile error. Inferred types are enforced exactly like written annotations, and the check happens before the code runs.

questions.question: What type does TypeScript infer for direction? Write the type exactly.
questions.code: const direction = "left";
questions.explanation: A const can never be reassigned, so TypeScript gives it the narrowest type: the literal type "left". With let it would widen to string, because a later assignment could change the value.

questions.question: Why is it common to annotate function parameters but not most local variables?
choices: Local variables cannot have type annotations
Annotations on local variables slow down the compiled JavaScript
Parameters are type checked at runtime, locals are not
A local's type is inferred from its initial value, but nothing tells the compiler what callers will pass
questions.explanation: Inference works from values. let total = 0 already says number, but a parameter has no value until a call happens, so without an annotation it is implicitly any, which strict mode reports. Types are erased when compiling, so they never affect runtime speed or checks.

questions.question: Which of these can a type alias do that an interface cannot?
choices: Name a union, such as string | number
Describe an object with optional properties
Mark a property as readonly
Be used as a function parameter type
questions.explanation: An interface always describes an object shape. A type alias can name any type, including unions, tuples and primitives. Optional and readonly properties, and use as a parameter type, work the same with both.

questions.question: Why does the last line fail to compile?
choices: p is declared with const, so none of its properties can change
Point needs a constructor before its properties can be set
x is readonly, so it cannot be assigned after the object is created
Interface fields cannot be changed to a different number
questions.explanation: readonly forbids assignment to that property: Cannot assign to 'x' because it is a read-only property. const only stops p from being reassigned; without readonly, p.x = 5 would compile.

questions.question: Complete the interface so a User can be created without an email.
questions.explanation: A ? after the property name makes it optional, and its type becomes string | undefined. The ! modifier is for definite assignment in classes and is a syntax error in an interface, and - and + are not valid here.

questions.question: What is the type of value on the line marked here?
questions.explanation: The if branch returns for every string, so only number is left on the last line. TypeScript follows the early return, which is why toFixed is allowed without a second check.

questions.question: Why is this a compile error?
choices: toUpperCase is not a real string method
The function needs an explicit return type
Unions cannot be used as parameter types
value might be a number, which has no toUpperCase; narrow it with typeof first
questions.explanation: On a union you can only use members that every type in it has. toUpperCase exists on string but not on number, so the error is Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'string | number'. Inside if (typeof value === "string") the call is allowed.

questions.question: Why can the last line use s.side without an error?
choices: TypeScript ignores property errors on union types
Every Shape has a side property
Returning early for "circle" leaves only the square member, which has side
The ** operator converts s to a number
questions.explanation: kind is a literal field that differs between the members, so checking it narrows s. After the circle case returns, s can only be the square member. Not every Shape has side: on an un-narrowed Shape, s.side is an error.

questions.question: Complete the declaration so first works with any element type and returns that same type.
choices: : T
questions.explanation: Type parameters are declared in angle brackets right after the function name. Without <T>, the compiler reports Cannot find name 'T', and the other forms are not valid syntax in that position.

questions.question: What type does TypeScript infer for x?
questions.explanation: The argument is a string[], so T is inferred as string and the return type T | undefined becomes string | undefined. The undefined is there because the array might be empty.

questions.question: Why does this generic function fail to compile?
choices: Generic functions cannot compare values
Nothing is known about T, so .length is not allowed; constrain it with <T extends { length: number }>
T must be replaced with any for property access to work
A ternary expression cannot return a generic type
questions.explanation: T could be any type, including number, which has no length, so the compiler reports Property 'length' does not exist on type 'T'. A constraint keeps the function generic while guaranteeing length exists. Switching to any would compile but lose the link between input and output types.

questions.question: What does a generic type parameter give you that typing the same function with any does not?
questions.answer: A generic keeps the connection between input and output types, so the caller gets back a precise type, such as string from a string[]. With any, the result is any and type checking stops there.
questions.explanation: Both versions accept many types, but only the generic remembers which type was passed in, so mistakes after the call are still caught.

questions.question: What does the compiler report for this code?
questions.code:
const data: unknown = JSON.parse('"hello"');
data.toUpperCase();
choices: Nothing; unknown allows any property access
Nothing at compile time, but a TypeError at runtime
Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'string'.
'data' is of type 'unknown'.
questions.explanation: unknown accepts any value but allows almost nothing until you narrow it, so the call is a compile error (TS18046). With any it would compile silently. The value really is a string here, but the compiler cannot know that without a typeof check.

questions.question: Which call compiles?
choices: updateUser(1, { email: "ada@example.com" })
updateUser(1, { age: 36 })
updateUser(1, { email: 42 })
updateUser(1, "ada@example.com")
questions.explanation: Partial<User> makes every property optional but keeps the property names and types, so passing only email is fine. age is not a User property, email must still be a string, and a bare string is not a matching object.

questions.question: Complete the annotation for an object whose keys are names and whose values are scores.
questions.code: const scores: _____ = { ada: 90, linus: 85 };
choices: Record<number, string>
Pick<string, number>
Record<string, number>
Partial<number>
questions.explanation: Record<K, V> is an object with keys of type K and values of type V, so string keys and number values is Record<string, number>. Record<number, string> has the two swapped, and Pick selects properties from an existing type rather than describing a map.

questions.question: Which utility type fills the blank so UserCard has only the id and name properties of User?
questions.code:
interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string }

type UserCard = _____<User, "id" | "name">;
questions.explanation: Pick<T, Keys> keeps only the listed keys of T. Omit with the same arguments would do the opposite and leave only email.

questions.question: What happens to type annotations when tsc compiles TypeScript to JavaScript?
choices: They become runtime checks that throw on wrong types
They are erased, and the output is plain JavaScript
They are kept as comments for the browser to read
They make the resulting JavaScript run faster
questions.explanation: Type checking happens only at compile time. The emitted JavaScript has no types and no added checks, which is why data from outside still needs runtime validation.

questions.question: Does the last line compile?
choices: Yes, because spot has every property Point requires
No: spot was never declared as a Point
No: Object literal may only specify known properties
Yes, but label is deleted when show runs
questions.explanation: TypeScript is structural: spot has a number x and y, so it is a valid Point, and the extra label is fine. The excess property check only applies to an object literal written directly where the type is expected. Nothing is deleted at runtime.

questions.question: This call is an error, yet passing the same object through a variable compiles. Why?
choices: Point would have to be a class to accept extra properties
Numbers can't be passed inside object literals
Object literals written directly where a type is expected get an excess property check, since extra properties there are usually typos
show needs a return type annotation first
questions.explanation: The error is TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'z' does not exist in type 'Point'. A fresh literal can only be used here, so an unknown property is most likely a mistake. A variable may be used elsewhere, so structural typing allows the extras.

questions.question: What type does TypeScript infer for ids?
questions.code: const ids = [1, 2, 3];
questions.explanation: Every element is a number, so the array is number[]. The array is still mutable (push works), so the elements widen to number rather than the literals 1, 2 and 3.

questions.question: What is the type of config.mode?
questions.code: const config = { mode: "dark" };
choices: "dark"
any
readonly "dark"
string
questions.explanation: const stops config from being rebound, but config.mode = "light" is still allowed, so the property widens to string. Writing { mode: "dark" } as const would give the readonly literal type "dark".

questions.question: Complete the annotation for a callback that takes a number and returns nothing useful.
questions.code: const onDone: _____ = (count) => console.log(count);
choices: Function<number, void>
(count: number) => void
(count): number => void
void (count: number)
questions.explanation: A function type lists named, typed parameters, then an arrow and the return type. With it, count is inferred as number inside the arrow. The other forms aren't valid TypeScript function types.

questions.question: Why does this fail to compile?
choices: string is not a valid return type
score must be annotated as an integer
An if statement can't contain a return
When score is below 90 the function returns nothing, but the return type promises a string
questions.explanation: TypeScript checks every path: falling off the end returns undefined, which isn't a string. The error is TS2366: Function lacks ending return statement and return type does not include 'undefined'. Add a final return.

questions.question: Inside this function, what is the type of name?
questions.explanation: An optional parameter may be left out, in which case it is undefined. You must handle that case before calling string methods on it.

questions.question: A teammate adds a triangle member to Shape but doesn't update this switch. What does the compiler do?
choices: Nothing: triangles silently return undefined at runtime
It reports that the switch needs a case for every string
It reports that the triangle member is not assignable to type 'never' on the default line
It removes triangle from the union automatically
questions.explanation: In the default branch, shape has been narrowed to whatever wasn't handled. Before the change that was nothing, so never fit. Now it's the triangle member, and assigning it to never is an error that points straight at the switch to update.

questions.question: Complete the condition so each branch can call its method.
choices: "swim" in animal
animal is Fish
typeof animal === "Fish"
animal instanceof Fish
questions.explanation: The in operator checks for a property at runtime, and TypeScript narrows on it. Fish is only a type, so instanceof Fish fails (it only refers to a type), typeof never returns "Fish", and animal is Fish is only valid as a return type annotation.

questions.question: Why does the last line fail to compile under strict mode?
choices: find can only be used on arrays of numbers
find returns User | undefined, so user is possibly undefined; check it or use user?.name
user must be declared with let
name is a reserved word in TypeScript
questions.explanation: When no element matches, find returns undefined, and the type says so. The error is TS18048: 'user' is possibly 'undefined'. Here it would have crashed at runtime, since there is no user with id 3.

questions.question: What does the ! in el!.textContent do?
choices: Checks at runtime and throws a clear error if el is null
Converts el to a boolean
Tells the compiler to treat el as non-null, with no check at runtime
Makes textContent optional
questions.explanation: The non-null assertion only silences the compiler; it is erased like every other type feature. If el really is null, the code crashes with the usual TypeError.

questions.question: What is the type of shown?
questions.explanation: ?? replaces undefined (and null) with the fallback, so whichever side is used, the result is a string. That's why ?? is a clean way to remove undefined from a type.

questions.question: What type does TypeScript infer for w?
questions.explanation: T is inferred from the argument as string, so the return type T[] becomes string[]. No explicit wrap<string> is needed.

questions.question: Match each compiler error to its most likely cause.

pairs.left: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
pairs.right: Storing a value of the wrong type

pairs.left: Property 'nmae' does not exist on type 'User'.
pairs.right: A typo in a property name
A parameter with no annotation under strict mode
Using a value that might be missing without checking

pairs.left: Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'.
pairs.right: Calling a function with the wrong argument type

questions.explanation: These five cover most day-to-day TypeScript errors. Read the first line, find the exact value or property it names, and fix that rather than silencing it.

questions.question: user has type User | undefined. Which of these handle it safely, without just silencing the compiler? Select all that apply.
choices: if (user) { console.log(user.name); }
console.log(user?.name);
console.log(user?.name ?? "guest");
console.log(user!.name);
console.log((user as any).name);
questions.explanation: A check, optional chaining and a ?? fallback all handle the missing case at runtime. The ! assertion and as any only stop the compiler from complaining, and both crash when user really is undefined.

questions.question: If TypeScript's types disappear at runtime, what do they buy you?
questions.answer: The compiler catches whole classes of bugs before the code runs: typos, wrong argument types, possibly undefined values and callers missed in a refactor. Types also power editor autocomplete and act as documentation that can't go stale.
questions.explanation: The value is all at development time. At runtime you still validate untrusted data, because the compiler never sees it.
